extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians interested in foundations and heuristic methods, graduate students and researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Cellucci's heuristic conception to evaluate or present mathematical research: emphasize discovery, analytic (backward) methods, openness, and the heuristic processes that generate results and subsequent problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-solving primacy (solves a non-trivial problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of mathematical work should solve a non-trivial problem; problem-solving is the primary measure of mathematical quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cellucci emphasizes that good mathematics is first and foremost aimed at solving substantive problems rather than merely elaborating axioms. Anti-pattern: work that only rephrases trivial consequences of definitions or reduces to routine exercise-like manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness (generates new problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong mathematical contribution generates new problems and lines of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fruitfulness is valued over final closure: good results open questions that lead to further discovery. Scoring guidance: prefer results that suggest multiple generalizations, variants, or unexpected connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduces methods of discovery, not just methods of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should present methods that aid discovery (heuristics), not merely formal techniques for justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cellucci distinguishes methods of discovery (analogy, generalization, specialization, working backward, conjecture-and-test) from mere proof tactics. Authors should make these heuristic moves explicit rather than hiding them in polished proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveals the analytic chain (analytic provenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition should show the analytic method — the backward chain of hypotheses leading from the goal to accepted assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from classical analytic method (start from conclusion, find hypotheses that imply it, continue until accepted premises). A piece that shows its analytic provenance is more comprehensible and easier to extend. Anti-pattern: presenting only the synthetic reorganization that obscures the discovery path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separates and addresses both logic of discovery and logic of justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation should consider both how results were discovered (heuristic process) and how they are justified (deductive proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cellucci insists the two are distinct: deductive logic is necessary but insufficient. Prefer papers that explicitly present both the discovery story and the formal justification, so readers can use the heuristic for further work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness about non-deductive methods (analogy, induction, abduction, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should use and acknowledge non-deductive heuristic methods (analogy, induction, abduction, generalization, specialization, working backward, conjecture-and-test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make heuristic techniques explicit rather than 'smuggling' them into arguments. Examples: explain analogies that suggested a conjecture, show how specialization led to a counterexample. Anti-pattern: pretending every step was purely deductive when heuristics produced the ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledges hypothetical/conditional character of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical statements should be presented as conditional on explicit hypotheses rather than as absolute certainties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cellucci stresses conditionality: results depend on hypotheses and may be revised. Guidance: clearly state hypotheses, discuss their role and possible relaxation. Anti-pattern: presenting results as unconditional truths without hypothesis discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connects to non-mathematical experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuable mathematics connects to physical, computational, philosophical, or broader intellectual experience rather than remaining isolated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cellucci (following Arnold) opposes disconnection from other intellectual life. Prefer work that explains applications, intuitions from modeling, computational experiments, or philosophical relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended problem orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should be oriented toward open problems and the exploratory investigation of uncertain territory rather than completion of closed exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage framing problems as open-ended, showing larger agendas and research programs. Anti-pattern: framing research as finishing a closed textbook exercise or merely filling a pre-specified slot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toleration of provisional results (Lakatosian quasi-proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept provisional or fallible results (conjectures, quasi-proofs) as productive steps in mathematical discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cellucci draws on Lakatos: quasi-proofs and provisional claims can drive progress. Guidance: permit and document tentative arguments, partial results, and refutations that illuminate the subject, instead of discarding them as 'incorrect' finished work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to revise definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical practice should allow definitions to be revised in light of progress and new insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cellucci endorses changing definitions when they obstruct discovery or fail to capture phenomena. Good work explains why a definition is adopted or modified, and how alternatives were considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of fallibility in proofs and conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that proofs and conjectures are fallible; treat mathematics as corrigible rather than absolutely certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows Cellucci's critique of foundational certainty. Guidance: document known gaps, dependencies on unproven assumptions, and openness to refutation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose heuristic provenance rather than hiding it in polished synthetic presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer expositions that make clear how discoveries were made rather than only providing tidy synthetic proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cellucci argues the finished synthetic proof is often a reorganization not the discovery. Authors should include the exploratory steps, failed attempts, heuristics, and motivations that led to the final form so readers can reproduce or extend the discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to foundationalist exclusivity (avoid claiming absolute certainty/deduction-only legitimacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid rhetoric or presentation that treats deduction as the only legitimate mathematical method or mathematics as absolutely certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cellucci critiques foundationalist assumptions: certainty and deduction-only norms. In practice, value and credit should be given to heuristic, informal, and empirical aspects of mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize methods that aid further investigation (plan-based understanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer contributions that provide 'plans' or algorithms of thought that others can reuse to discover related results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects to Hamami & Morris: plan-based accounts of understanding. Good papers include explicit plans, heuristics, and strategies that make the subject tractable for further work.
